definition.text: Longshore drift is the transport of sediment (clay, silt, pebbles, sand, shingle, shells) along a coast parallel to the shoreline, depending on the angle of incoming waves.

facts.text: Oblique incoming wind squeezes water along the coast, creating a current parallel to it; the sediment this current moves is longshore drift, within the surf zone.
Breaking surf sends water up the beach (swash) at an oblique angle and gravity drains it straight downslope (backwash), also moving beach sand.

Early 20th-century oceanographers and coastal engineers found the angle of wave approach paramount, leading to the longshore current concept and the drift-aligned beach, with deposition on one side and erosion on the other.
The first scientific studies of coastal sediment movement began in the mid-1800s, before the term longshore drift existed.
A slight change in sediment supply or wind direction can change drift dramatically, altering how a beach forms and evolves.

definition.text: A sediment budget accounts for the sediment sources and sinks within a coastal system.

facts.text: Sediment from any source enters the coastal system and is transported by longshore drift; artificial sinks include mining or extraction.
Inlet ebb-tidal shoals illustrate budget and drift working together, storing sand moved by longshore transport.

definition.text: Spits and barriers are landforms built where longshore drift deposits sediment, a spit being attached to land at one end and a barrier at both.

facts.text: A spit forms where drift passes a point, such as a river mouth, at which the dominant drift direction and shoreline do not veer the same way; its distal end is detached and may hook.
Barrier systems may enclose an estuary or lagoon, as the Kaitorete Spit does for Lake Ellesmere / Te Waihora.
Tidal inlets on drift shores accumulate sediment in flood and ebb shoals and act as sinks and sources; an unstructured inlet lets sediment by-pass and form bars down-drift.

definition.text: A detached breakwater is a shore protection structure built to build up sandy material between it and the coast.

facts.text: It has no connection to the shoreline, letting currents and sediment pass between structure and shore, to accommodate storm drawdown.
It creates a zone of reduced wave energy that encourages sand deposition on its lee side.

title: Ports and harbours effect on drift
article: Longshore drift#Human influences > Ports and harbours

definition.text: Ports and harbours can seriously disrupt natural longshore drift by altering sedimentation patterns.

facts.text: The altered sedimentation can cause accretion or erosion of a beach or coastal system, and threatens longer-term shoreline evolution.
The late 19th-century port at Timaru, New Zealand, blocked coarse sediment drifting north and made it accrete south of the port at South beach.
